title: Event Delivery Models and Guarantees
readerIntent: Choose local, transported, or persisted delivery and state its guarantees honestly.
summary: A local listener call is not durable messaging; each event contract states locality, persistence, acknowledgement, ordering, redelivery, idempotency, retry, and recovery behavior.

sections.heading: Delivery choices
items: Local listener: low overhead inside the runtime process; not durable by itself.
Broker transport: crosses processes through a configured adapter; guarantees depend on the provider and configuration.
Persisted NEMS distribution: records definitions, outcomes, failure state, retry, and event logs.
Workflow or scheduled job: preferred when work is long-running, human-involved, timed, or requires explicit business state.

sections.heading: Contract questions
items: Is delivery best effort, at-most-once, at-least-once, or otherwise qualified?
Must ordering be preserved and at what partition scope?
How does a consumer detect and safely handle redelivery?
Who owns retry, dead-letter or failed state, replay, and manual recovery?
What tenant, source, target, trace, schema version, and security context travels with the event?

sections.heading: Provider maturity
paragraphs: A broker adapter is production-qualified only with live evidence for its claimed acknowledgement, ordering, redelivery, security, outage, recovery, capacity, and upgrade behavior. A module scaffold or unit test does not establish those guarantees.

sections.heading: At-least-once implications
paragraphs: At-least-once delivery means a consumer can receive the same event again after timeout, reconnect, crash, or replay. The consumer uses stable event and business identities and records or derives idempotent completion.
Acknowledgement occurs only after the consumer reaches its documented completion boundary.

sections.heading: Ordering and partitions
paragraphs: Global ordering is expensive and rarely necessary. Define the narrow key—such as one stock item, workflow, or aggregate—where order matters. Consumers still handle duplicates and stale versions.
Parallel partitions improve throughput but require capacity, rebalance, and poison-message strategy.

sections.heading: Commands, facts, and workflows
items: A fact reports a completed authoritative transition.
A command requests an owner to attempt behavior and needs an explicit result contract.
A workflow coordinates durable business actions and waiting.
Do not disguise a synchronous API requirement as an event when the caller needs immediate success or failure.

sections.heading: Delivery acceptance tests
items: Success, duplicate, redelivery, out-of-order, and stale version.
Consumer crash before and after completion.
Broker loss, partition, reconnect, and backlog recovery.
Unauthorized publisher, destination, tenant, or payload.
Poison message, retry exhaustion, replay, and manual recovery.
Shutdown and upgrade without silent loss.
